items.title: Anthropic and OpenAI are coming for the development workflow | InfoWorld
items.summary: This is clearly where the frontier labs are moving, even though they’ve all benefited from an industry that provided neutral spaces to build. For example, OpenAI developed Pando, a Git back end for its own monorepo, to handle more engineers and agents reading and writing code concurrently. Its engineers kept using Git. OpenAI retained compatibility with the protocol and client and contributed improvements upstream. That compatibility let it rebuild the back end around the way its engineers [...] This pressure to maximize profitability helps explain why frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI are aggressively adding functionality to own more of the developer’s workflow. On November 4, OpenAI announced an agreement to buy Pierre, the company behind Code Storage and the open source libraries Codex already uses to browse files and review changes. OpenAI wants Codex to be where developers work, from the first branch an agent creates through deployment of the application. There’s money in [...] OpenAI or Anthropic could build the place developers prefer to work. The question is what happens when a team likes that place and wants a rival’s agent for a particular job. Maybe a startup has built a tool that can track down the intermittent test failure that’s had the team stumped for a week. Give it access to the code and test history the team has authorized, and it gets a chance to prove itself. Ask the team to move its work to a new platform first, and it probably never gets to try.

My roommate hasn't slept since this shit... Claude Code just found a one-person website that made $4,800 in a single day. The guy who runs it has 27 followers on X, and he's selling the whole business for $360.

It finds local businesses with no website, builds each one a site with AI in minutes and writes the pitch for you. A web agency you run alone from a laptop.

This wasn't a screenshot from some guru. Every dollar was read straight from Stripe on TrustMRR, with the day it landed: $0 for 22 days, then $4,800 on one day. 48 people visited the site that whole month.

He opened Claude Code on his MacBook, made a folder called steal and told it to pull the 25 fastest-growing businesses on TrustMRR with $1,000 to $20,000 of checked revenue last month. 10 names came back, and 8 never said where their customers come from.

He started scrolling. A library of AI agent skills went from $27 in August to $12,216 in October, paid every single day. An email app for Mac went from $238 to $23,099 in one month. Then he opened the listing for the $4,800 site: "375 interested buyers saw this recently." People were lining up to buy it while he was still reading.

Tiny businesses that make money don't need an audience, so nobody posts about them. Their numbers sit on a public page that almost nobody reads.

Claude Code only runs this while his laptop is awake, so he gave the same job to viktor, an AI employee in his Slack that works from its own computer in the cloud. Every Monday it sends him the new winners and a steal sheet for the best one.

He copied the website-for-local-shops one that weekend. By Friday four shops had paid him $400 each for sites he never designed. How many people are already copying the same 10 businesses, I don't know.

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: run Sonnet, Haiku and Opus 5.5 together, each one doing only the job it's best at.

Opus-level judgment on every big call, without paying Opus rates for every routine turn.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model sonnet --advisor opus

here's the split:

→ Sonnet 5.5 runs the session and writes the code
→ Haiku 5.5 explores files and docs in parallel
→ Opus 5.5 stays on call as advisor for the big calls
→ you stop spending Opus on work that doesn't need it

Opus only steps in at three moments:

→ before a plan locks
→ when the same error shows up twice
→ before calling it done

Sonnet builds. Haiku explores. Opus reviews.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file, which tool, retry or stop) go to JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that split

the full tree
> Sonnet 5.5 runs the main session and edits code
> search maps the repo on Haiku 5.5
> grep finds call sites on Haiku 5.5
> docs pulls the API reference on Haiku 5.5
> Opus 5.5 on call as advisor, reads the whole transcript when consulted

items.title: Scaling AI-driven chip design with open agent factories - IBM Research
items.summary: AI for chip design connects two forms of progress into a reciprocal relationship: Better hardware enables more capable AI, and more capable AI can help engineers develop better hardware. Cost-efficient agent factories make that relationship more practical. By making each search more affordable, open models and distributed inference create room to test more ideas and, with better search strategies, turn that opportunity into better chips. [...] As AI systems become more capable, researchers are increasingly asking a practical question: Can AI do more than help write code for computing systems? Specifically, can it actively participate in the design of complex computing systems and rapidly translate algorithms into silicon? New work in AI-driven chip design suggests the answer is yes. But a promising algorithm is only the beginning of a hardware design. Turning it into an efficient chip requires exploring how to organize computation, [...] The results also suggest that the practical value of AI-assisted chip design depends on more than the best design an agent can produce. It also depends on how much verified exploration an organization can afford. Model capability, the assignment of agent roles, and the infrastructure serving those models all shape the hardware improvements that are attainable within a real engineering budget. By combining open frontier models with llm-d’s low-cost distributed inference, IBM has demonstrated

items.title: Microsoft will mainly use its Maia chips for AI inference
items.summary:
The emerging opportunity in chips stems from unrelenting demand for advanced processors and a desire in the market for choice. Nvidia's GPUs have been the standard for AI workloads and models, and they fill Microsoft's existing data centers, while also serving to train models from OpenAI and Anthropic.

But as demand keeps growing, the model leaders have embraced a variety of silicon from companies including Amazon, Advanced Micro Devices, Cerebras, Google and, in recent months, Microsoft. [...] Microsoft introduced its inaugural AI chip, the Maia 100, in 2023. It touted the Maia 200 this past January, and CEO Satya Nadella told analysts in July that Maia 200 "delivers 30% better performance per dollar than the latest generation hardware in our fleet" and said it was handling OpenAI models. [...] In this article

Microsoft will ramp up use of its homegrown artificial intelligence chips after years of reliance on Nvidia's graphics processing units, as the software giant attempts to bolster its AI stack.

Starting with its third-generation Maia AI accelerator, unveiled on Monday, Microsoft said it will mainly rely on its own silicon to handle incoming requests.
